{{inline citations needed|date=June 2024}}

In [[mathematics]], a '''Nakayama algebra''' or '''generalized uniserial algebra''' is an [[algebra over a field|algebra]] such that each left or right [[indecomposable module|indecomposable]] [[projective module]] has a unique [[composition series]]. They were studied by {{harvs|txt|first=Tadasi |last=Nakayama|authorlink=Tadasi Nakayama|year=1940}} who called them "generalized uni-serial rings". These algebras were further studied by {{harvs|txt|first=Herbert|last=Kupisch|authorlink=Herbert Kupisch|year=1959}} and later by {{harvs|txt|first=Ichiro|last=Murase|year=1963-64}}, by {{harvs|txt|first=Kent Ralph|last=Fuller|year=1968}} and by {{harvs|txt|first=Idun|last=Reiten|year=1982}}.

An example of a Nakayama algebra is ''k''[''x'']/(''x''<sup>''n''</sup>) for ''k'' a [[field (mathematics)|field]] and ''n'' a positive [[integer]]. 

Current usage of ''uniserial'' differs slightly: an explanation of the difference appears [[Serial module#Notes on alternate, similar and related terms|here]].
